demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Vignette: Mara

Mara is forty-six years old, a forensic analyst for the city's medical examiner's office. She has been married to her husband, Tomas, for nineteen years. They have two children, both in their late teens.

The event happened fourteen months ago. Mara's younger brother, Keahi, died in a single-car accident on a rain-slicked highway. He was thirty-eight, a commercial fisherman, broad-shouldered and quick to laugh. The call came at two in the morning. Mara remembers the way the kitchen light flickered as she grabbed her keys. She remembers the wet asphalt under her boots at the scene, the paramedics already pulling a tarp over the driver's side. She did not see his face, but she saw his hand-the same scar on his thumb from a childhood fishing hook-and she knew.

That night changed the rhythm of her breathing.

Now, when Mara walks into the lab, she sees the rows of stainless steel drawers that hold the bodies of strangers. She works with evidence from homicides and suspicious deaths-analyzing trace fibers, gunshot residue, blood spatter patterns. The work used to feel like a puzzle, a way to bring clarity to chaos. Now every case whispers Keahi's name. Last week she caught herself staring at a photograph of a man's hands, the tendons and calluses so familiar she had to set down her magnifying lens and walk outside. Her supervisor asked if she was feeling ill. She said she was fine.

She is not fine.

Mara wakes most nights around three, the same hour the phone rang. Her chest seizes. She lies still, afraid to move, because movement might mean getting out of bed and walking toward another door she doesn't want to open. Tomas reaches for her. She stiffens. Intimacy feels like a country she can no longer find the map to. She used to love the weight of his arm across her waist. Now it reminds her of the tarp, of weight that is no longer alive.

Driving to work is its own ordeal. The highway curves near the same overpass where Keahi's truck left the road. Mara takes alternate routes now, even if it adds forty minutes. When she has no choice but to drive that stretch-when a case requires her to be at a scene on the north side-her hands sweat so badly she has to grip the wheel with both fists. The windshield wipers, even in dry weather, can trigger a full panic attack: the stutter of rubber on glass, the blur of headlights. She once pulled over and vomited into a drainage ditch.

At work, her colleagues do not know the full story. She is professional, efficient. She reviews toxicology reports and autopsy notes without visible emotion. But the details lodge themselves inside her. Decomposition rates. Ligature marks. The angle of a fracture. She used to be able to compartmentalize-it was part of the job. Now every piece of trauma feels like it belongs to her brother. She finds herself checking the names, hoping for a stranger, and hating herself for the relief when the name is unfamiliar.

Her family notices. Her daughter asked last month why she never laughs anymore. Her son told Tomas that Mom seems "spaced out." Mara has started forgetting things: appointments, whether she locked the car, what day it is. Yesterday she found herself standing in the kitchen holding the phone, the number for Keahi's voicemail already dialed. She hung up before it rang.

She does not talk about the accident. When friends offer condolences, she changes the subject. When Tomas brings up grief counseling, she says she's managing. The truth is that she does not want to speak the story aloud, because speaking it makes it real again, and real means she has to feel the full weight of it. She already feels it in her body: the constant knot in her stomach, the headache that presses behind her eyes every afternoon, the tremor in her hands when she tries to write a report.

Mara still does her job. She is good at it. But she works slower now, rereading notes three times, double-checking calculations. She is terrified of making a mistake-of missing a detail that costs another family what hers has lost. That fear, she knows, is unreasonable. She also knows it will not leave.
